editor_spans.body: The speech in Motherwell names the wrong culprit for its own case study. Burnham uses Ravenscraig as the emblem of distant decisions wrecking a community. But the steelworks did not close because Lanarkshire lacked a say over employment support or skills budgets. It closed because the decisions that mattered, about capital, ownership and demand for steel, were made at national and market level. A regional authority with an employability budget could not have saved it.

The concrete offer has the same mismatch. What Burnham proposes to hand down is the social-repair end of the economy: localised employment support, employability and enterprise funding, and a say over a slice of R&D spending. The levers he credits with actual reindustrialisation stay with the centre: shipbuilding and defence orders, Grangemouth, energy jobs, the £1 billion research budget and a UK-wide procurement rule. 'Push power out' mostly means devolving the work of helping people adapt to industrial decisions that are still taken centrally.

His procurement pitch also carries a cost he names only in passing. As mayor he paid 'a little more' to buy Falkirk-built buses. Turned into a rule for all public buying, that is a standing premium on public budgets. It sits awkwardly beside a closer trade relationship with the EU, which he is pursuing at the same time. The 20 November summit will show which of the two commitments gives way.

The tone of cooperation comes with a deadline attached. He calls Holyrood's local government reform too slow and warns that Scottish towns could become 'underpowered' while northern English cities power up. That turns English devolution into a yardstick the SNP government will be judged against. The National Economic Council meeting, the first since he took office, is where that pressure becomes a public test.
